title: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
goal: Given a production stem about configuration, workflow or CI, decide whether the standard must be ambient or invoked, whether decisions remain, and which mechanism enforces it, then pick the option that matches instead of the trap.

steps.title: Three developers, one dissenter
steps.lead: Start with the failure, not the theory. Four developers, same repository, same branch, and only one of them gets the behaviour everyone agreed on. Before anything gets named, notice what the stem already told you about where that instruction lives.
points: Three developers say Claude follows the team rule on comprehensive error handling. A fourth, who joined last week, sees none of it.
All four have up-to-date clones of the same branch, so the guidance cannot be sitting in the repository.
That single fact decides most questions in this domain: guidance everyone must receive has to travel through version control.
Anything stored under `~/.claude/` is personal and is never carried by git.
steps.caption: Both panels hold the same rule; only the right one sits in the repository, which is why git never delivered it.
steps.takeaway: If one developer gets different behaviour, the instruction is in a home directory, not the repo.

steps.title: The path prefix is the whole answer
steps.lead: Here is the rule that answers more Domain 3 questions than any other. Same filename, opposite scope, and the only difference is the path prefix. `~/.claude/` is personal; `.claude/` is the project and travels through git.
points: Loading runs broad to specific: managed policy, then user, then project, then local, then directory files on demand.
Managed policy is admin-controlled and cannot be excluded. Your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is personal and not version-controlled.
`./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` is the committed project file, the only one teammates receive.
`./CLAUDE.local.md` holds personal project preferences and is gitignored.
Directory files scope downward and local only: `src/backend/CLAUDE.md` does not change work done in `src/`.
steps.caption: Read the first column for the prefix and the last for reach: only the checked-in project files ever leave your machine.
steps.code:
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md        personal, never shared
./CLAUDE.md                project, committed, shared
./.claude/CLAUDE.md        same as above
./CLAUDE.local.md          personal, gitignored
<subdir>/CLAUDE.md         on demand, scopes downward only
steps.takeaway: `~/.claude/` is yours alone. `.claude/` is the team's. Same name, opposite reach.

steps.title: Five layers, narrowing as they descend
steps.lead: Read the hierarchy as layers that get more specific as they get closer to the work. Files in the working directory and its ancestors load at launch; files in subtrees below load on demand, when Claude reads files in those subtrees.
points: Managed policy sits at the top and no setting can remove it.
User file next: personal, invisible to teammates, never committed.
Project file next: committed, shared, the one the team actually receives.
Local file next: personal overrides for this one repository, gitignored.
Directory files last and on demand, scoped downward and local.
steps.caption: Follow it top to bottom: broad at the top, specific at the bottom, and only the project layer reaches a teammate.
steps.takeaway: Broad at the top, specific at the bottom, and only the project layer travels with the repo.

steps.title: Gate: the new developer who sees nothing
steps.lead: Answer it now, before the rest of the lesson. One detail in the stem rules out two of the options for you.
steps.caption: Match cause before choosing a fix: a clone that is already current rules out anything stored in the repository.

ask.q: Your team has used Claude Code on the same repo for months. Three developers report that Claude follows the team's guidance to always include comprehensive error handling, but a fourth developer who joined last week says Claude ignores it. All four have up-to-date clones of the same branch. Which approach is most effective?
options: Have the new developer delete the conflicting section from their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
Move the guidance from the original developers' user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and commit it.
Tell the new developer to repeat the requirement in prompts until Claude remembers it for their sessions.
Clear the Claude Code cache on all four machines so the current instructions are re-read.
ask.why: Personal configuration in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is never carried by git, so teammates never receive it, and team standards belong in the version-controlled project file. Deleting a section of the new developer's own file assumes a conflict where the symptom is a missing instruction, repeating the requirement assumes per-user learning the product does not do, and clearing a cache assumes a cache that does not exist.

steps.takeaway: Personal files never reach a teammate. Team standards go in the committed project file.

steps.title: The layer nobody may opt out of
steps.inshort: Project file for the team; managed policy for the whole org and for rules no team can waive.
steps.lead: A security team mandates that every repository in the company runs the internal scan before a commit, and no team may weaken it. Reach for a project file and each team can edit or delete it in the next PR. The judgment is not only where a rule is shared, but who is allowed to not follow it.
points: Managed policy (enterprise) sits above every other layer, is admin-controlled, and cannot be excluded or overridden.
The project `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is the team's shared layer, but the team owns it, so it can be changed in a commit.
The user file `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies to all of one person's projects and reaches no teammate.
`./CLAUDE.local.md` is one person's override for one repo, gitignored, so it can never carry an org mandate.
Receipt map: managed policy reaches everyone in the org; the project file reaches everyone on the repo; user and local reach you alone.
steps.why: The exam separates 'must reach the team' from 'must reach everyone and cannot be waived'. The first is the committed project file; the second is the managed policy layer.
steps.contrast: Copying the mandate into each repository's project CLAUDE.md feels shared, but any team can delete it in the next commit, so it is not an org-wide requirement.
steps.exam: "Applies to all repositories", "cannot be overridden", "no team may opt out" point to managed policy, not the project file.
steps.takeaway: Project file for the team. Managed policy for the whole org and for anything nobody may opt out of.

steps.title: Gate: the rule no team may waive
steps.inshort: Org-wide and non-excludable means the managed policy layer.
steps.lead: One phrase in the stem decides it: teams must not be able to remove the requirement.

ask.q: Your organisation mandates that every repository runs the internal security scan before any commit, and individual teams must not be able to weaken or remove the requirement. Where should the instruction live?
options: In each repository's committed `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so every team pulls it with the code.
In the managed policy file at the OS-specific path, which is admin-controlled and cannot be excluded.
In each developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so it loads for every project they open.
In a `.claude/rules/` file with `paths:` frontmatter inside every repository.
ask.why: Managed policy cannot be excluded, so it holds even when a team would rather not follow it. The project file is shared but team-owned, so it can be edited or deleted in a commit; the user file reaches one developer only; and a rules file is still a project file the team controls.

steps.why: Non-excludable org-wide rules are the one case where the answer is not the project file.
steps.contrast: The project file feels like the safe shared home, but 'shared' is not 'mandatory'.
steps.exam: "Cannot be overridden" or "no team may opt out" is the managed-policy tell.
steps.takeaway: Team standard goes in the project file. Org mandate that cannot be waived goes in managed policy.

steps.title: Ambient standards and on-demand workflows
steps.lead: Now the category error the exam builds questions from. One mechanism loads in every session because the standard must always apply; the other loads only when someone invokes it. Choose the wrong one and you either burn context on every turn or quietly turn a standard into an option.
points: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded standards. A skill or a slash command is an on-demand workflow.
Commands merged into skills: `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` give `/deploy`; a skill wins a collision.
Priority is enterprise, then personal `~/.claude/skills/`, then project `.claude/skills/`, then plugins.
A skill body enters the conversation once, as standing instruction, and is not re-read on later turns. Write policy, not one-time steps.
Location and isolation are separate axes: a skill can be project-scoped and forked, or personal and unforked.
steps.caption: The left column loads itself and the right column waits to be invoked; only the top row is what the team receives.
steps.takeaway: Must happen every time is CLAUDE.md. Invoked when needed is a skill. Never swap them.

steps.title: Three frontmatter knobs the exam tests
steps.lead: A stem about a misbehaving skill almost always maps symptom to frontmatter. Three symptoms, three declarations, and every wrong option is advice where a declaration was needed.
points: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent, so verbose output stays out of the main conversation.
Must not modify anything: restrict `allowed-tools` to the operations the skill needs, so destructive tools are simply unavailable.
Invoked with no argument and produces junk: `argument-hint` prompts for the required parameter.
Personal variant of a team skill: a new name under `~/.claude/skills/`. Editing the team skill changes everyone.
A warning in the description is not a restriction, and prose validation inside `SKILL.md` is advisory, not enforcement.
steps.caption: Noisy means context: fork, unsafe means allowed-tools, missing input means argument-hint — and a warning is none of the three.
steps.takeaway: Noisy means `context: fork`, unsafe means `allowed-tools`, missing input means `argument-hint`.

steps.title: Gate: the skill with three symptoms
steps.lead: Three problems in one stem, which usually means three controls in one answer. Watch for the option that offers a warning instead of a restriction.
steps.caption: Three symptoms, three declarations: the left column restricts what can happen, the right column only asks nicely.

ask.q: Your team's `/migration` skill generates database migration files and takes the migration name via `$ARGUMENTS`. Three problems appear in production: developers run it with no arguments and get poorly named files; the skill sometimes picks up schema details from unrelated prior conversations; and a developer once triggered destructive test cleanup because the skill had broad tool access. Which approach is most effective?
options: Use positional `$1` and `$2` instead of `$ARGUMENTS`, add explicit schema file references with `@` syntax, and add a frontmatter description warning about destructive operations.
Split the skill into `/migration-create` and `/migration-apply` with different `allowed-tools` scopes.
Add prose validation in `SKILL.md` to check `$ARGUMENTS`, plus instructions to ignore prior conversation context and a list of prohibited operations.
Add `argument-hint` so a required parameter is requested, set `context: fork` to isolate execution, and restrict `allowed-tools` to the file-write operations the skill needs.
ask.why: Three problems map to three frontmatter controls: `argument-hint` for the missing argument, `context: fork` so prior conversation context does not leak in, and `allowed-tools` to make destructive tools unavailable. A description-level warning is advice rather than a restriction, splitting the skill leaves the missing-argument and context-leak problems unsolved, and prose validation is advisory where a declaration is required.

steps.takeaway: One symptom, one declaration. A warning is not a restriction.

steps.title: A skill is a folder; a command is a file
steps.inshort: A command is one static prompt file; a skill is a directory that can carry templates, references and its own tool scope.
steps.lead: Both are typed as `/name`, so from the keyboard they look identical, and the exam makes you justify which one a problem calls for. The difference is what each can carry and who decides when it runs.
points: A command is a single markdown file holding one static prompt; the same text runs every time you type its name.
A skill is a directory: `SKILL.md` is the router, and the folder can also ship `templates/` and a `reference.md` the skill pulls in, so it carries far more context.
A command runs only when a human types `/name`; a skill is also invoked on demand, but Claude can fire it automatically when its description matches the request.
Reach for a skill when the work is a multi-step procedure with its own context and tool needs; reach for a command when it is a reusable static prompt.
A fifty-step checklist sitting in `CLAUDE.md` loads into every session; the same checklist as a skill loads only when it is needed.
steps.why: The exam contrasts the three surfaces: CLAUDE.md is ambient, a command is an explicitly invoked static prompt, and a skill is an on-demand procedure that can carry supporting files and a restricted tool set.
steps.contrast: Dumping a long procedural checklist into CLAUDE.md feels like making it always available, but it pollutes every session with steps that rarely apply.
steps.exam: "Available to all contributors" means project scope; "multi-step procedure", "needs specific tools" or "runs on demand" means a skill.
steps.takeaway: Static reusable prompt is a command. Multi-step, tool-scoped, folder-backed procedure is a skill.

steps.title: Gate: static prompt or procedure
steps.inshort: Multi-step, tool-scoped work is a skill; a bloated checklist moves out of CLAUDE.md into one.
steps.lead: Two jobs in one stem: a fixed procedure the team runs every release, and a long checklist that is polluting every session.

ask.q: A team wants a reusable `/release-notes` action that reads the merged PRs, groups them by area, writes a changelog file and posts a summary, using only read and write tools. They also have a 40-step onboarding checklist currently pasted into the project `CLAUDE.md`, loaded in every session. Which approach is most effective?
options: Make `/release-notes` a skill in `.claude/skills/` with `allowed-tools` limited to the read and write tools it needs, and move the onboarding checklist out of `CLAUDE.md` into its own skill.
Make both a single `.claude/commands/` file each, since commands and skills behave identically.
Keep the onboarding checklist in `CLAUDE.md` and add `/release-notes` as a command so it stays simple.
Put `/release-notes` in `~/.claude/skills/` so it is available across the developer's own projects.
ask.why: A fixed multi-step procedure that needs a bounded tool set is a skill, and `allowed-tools` enforces least privilege; the 40-step checklist is a procedure that belongs in a skill so it stops loading into every session. Commands cannot carry supporting files or a tool scope, and leaving the checklist in `CLAUDE.md` keeps polluting every session. User scope is not shared, so the team would not receive `/release-notes`.

steps.why: The stem names a procedure, a tool restriction and a bloated ambient file; each maps to the same fix.
steps.contrast: Treating a procedure as a command is tempting because a command is quicker to write, but it cannot hold the steps, the tools or the supporting files.
steps.exam: "Multi-step procedure" plus "only these tools" is a skill with `allowed-tools`, not a command.
steps.takeaway: Procedure becomes a skill. Reusable prompt stays a command. Long checklists leave CLAUDE.md.

steps.title: A pattern of files, not a directory
steps.lead: Tests that sit next to the code they test. Migrations in four services. Terraform files in three trees. These are not directories, they are patterns, and a directory-level file cannot express a pattern.
points: The mechanism is a file in `.claude/rules/` whose frontmatter declares `paths:` globs such as `**/*.test.ts` or `src/api/**/*.ts`.
The rule loads only when Claude Code is about to work on a matching file, so unrelated work pays nothing for it.
Without frontmatter a rule file loads unconditionally at session start. Adding `paths:` is what makes loading conditional.
One glob-keyed rule applies to new directories automatically and cannot drift into several copies.
The example that keeps returning: one rule with `**/migrations/**/*` covers every current and future migrations directory.
steps.caption: Follow the globs: the rule fires only when Claude is about to work on a matching file, wherever that file lives.
steps.code:
---
paths:
  - "**/*.test.ts"
  - "**/migrations/**/*"
---
Migration rules: naming, reversibility, no data backfills in the same PR.
steps.takeaway: A convention for a file pattern is one `.claude/rules/` file with a `paths:` glob, never a copy per directory.

steps.title: Why not the root, why not a command
steps.lead: The same convention has four possible homes, and the exam makes you justify the one you chose. Each alternative is a real mechanism being used for the wrong shape of problem.
points: Root CLAUDE.md: always loaded, so it burns context during debugging and review where the convention is irrelevant.
A CLAUDE.md per directory: copies that drift, and it cannot reach tests that live outside that directory.
A slash command everyone must run first: an ambient standard turned opt-in. A command for a convention is always wrong.
A skill per code type: opt-in again, so the convention does not apply automatically as code is generated.
Reach for a rule when a path pattern decides; reach for a skill when a task, not a path, is the trigger.
steps.caption: Scan the right column: every alternative either loads where it is irrelevant or waits for someone to remember it.
steps.takeaway: Path pattern means a rule. Task trigger means a skill. A command means the standard became optional.

steps.title: Gate: conventions per code type
steps.lead: The stem gives you the decisive detail in its last sentence: identical conventions wherever the test files live. Now answer.
steps.caption: Watch it narrow: only the bottom stage reaches identical conventions wherever the test files happen to live.

ask.q: Conventions differ across your codebase: React components use functional style, API handlers use async/await with specific error handling, and models follow the repository pattern. Test files sit next to the code they test, such as `Button.test.tsx` beside `Button.tsx`, and must follow identical conventions wherever they live. Which approach is most effective?
options: Create rule files under `.claude/rules/` with YAML frontmatter declaring glob patterns, so conventions apply based on file path.
Put all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md under headings for each area and rely on Claude to infer which section applies.
Create a skill per code type with the conventions embedded in each `SKILL.md`.
Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each subdirectory holding that area's conventions.
ask.why: Glob-frontmatter rules apply a convention deterministically by path, including to test files distributed next to their source, which is exactly what a directory file cannot reach. Inference from headings is non-deterministic and fails when conventions overlap, a skill is opt-in so nothing applies automatically as code is generated, and one CLAUDE.md per subdirectory leaves the tests living outside those directories uncovered.

steps.takeaway: Globs follow the pattern. Directory files only follow the directory.

steps.title: Two globs, two meanings
steps.inshort: `*` matches one directory level; `**` matches any depth. That one difference decides whether a rule follows the pattern everywhere.
steps.lead: A rule is only as precise as its glob. The exam tests `*` against `**`, and the trap is a pattern that looks like it covers the tree but stops one level down.
points: `**` matches any number of directories, at any depth; `*` matches within a single directory level only.
`**/*.test.ts` is every test file anywhere; `src/api/*.ts` is only TypeScript files directly in `src/api`, not in its subfolders.
`terraform/**/*` is every file under `terraform` at any depth, which is why one rule covers directories that do not exist yet.
`paths:` globs are matched against the file Claude is about to work on, regardless of where in the tree it sits.
A pattern with a single `*` in the middle looks like it covers the tree but silently stops one level down.
steps.why: The conditional load is the whole value of a rule, and the glob decides which files trigger it. `**` is what lets one rule follow a pattern across the codebase; `*` anchors it to one level.
steps.contrast: A shorter glob such as `*/migrations/*` looks tidy, but it reaches only one directory deep and misses nested service folders.
steps.exam: When the stem says a pattern appears 'at any depth' or 'wherever it lives', the correct glob uses `**`.
steps.takeaway: `*` is one level. `**` is any depth. Use `**` when the pattern must follow the files.

steps.title: Gate: one directory or any depth
steps.inshort: The pattern must follow the files to a new, deeper location, so the glob needs `**`.
steps.lead: The stem tells you where the files live today and where they are about to appear. Read the depth, then choose the glob.

ask.q: Migration files currently live under `db/migrations/`, and the platform team is about to add `services/billing/db/migrations/` and `services/auth/db/migrations/`. One rule must apply to every migration file, present and future, wherever it lives. Which `paths:` entry is correct?
options: `db/migrations/*`
`**/migrations/**/*`
`*/migrations/*`
`db/**/migrations/*.sql`
ask.why: `**/migrations/**/*` matches a `migrations` directory at any depth and every file beneath it, so it follows the files into the new service trees automatically. `db/migrations/*` covers only the one existing tree; `*/migrations/*` reaches a single directory level, so `services/billing/db/migrations/` two levels down is missed; `db/**/migrations/*.sql` is anchored to `db/` and only matches `.sql`.

steps.why: A glob anchored to today's path or limited to one level cannot follow a pattern the stem says will move deeper.
steps.contrast: The narrow glob matches everything in the repository today, which is exactly why it passes review and then fails when the new directories appear.
steps.exam: "Wherever it lives" plus "any depth" is the `**` tell.
steps.takeaway: `**` follows the pattern. A single `*` stops at one level and misses the new folders.

steps.title: Decisions remaining, or known work
steps.lead: Plan mode is not a virtue and direct execution is not a shortcut. The dividing line is one question: are there decisions still to be made, or is the thing to do already known?
points: Plan mode triggers: multi-file changes, architectural decisions, several valid approaches, large scope, unclear requirements.
Direct execution triggers: a single-file fix with a clear stack trace, adding a null check, a stated mechanical edit.
A migration touching 45 or more files is not mechanical. Different APIs at each call site mean decisions remain.
The hybrid is valid and commonly tested: plan to investigate and design, get approval, then execute file by file.
Plan mode is workflow control gating thinking to doing. It is not extended thinking, which is a reasoning budget.
steps.caption: The dividing line runs across the top: decisions still to be made put you in plan mode whatever the size of the change.
steps.takeaway: Decisions remaining means plan mode. A known edit means execute. Repetitive edits are not known work.

steps.title: The mechanism behind the label
steps.lead: Know the surface behind the classification, because the exam also tests the flag. Plan mode is one entry in a permission-mode system, not a separate feature.
points: Select a mode with `--permission-mode <mode>`, or cycle the modes with `Shift+Tab`.
The modes are `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk` and `bypassPermissions`.
Plan mode explores read-only with Glob, Grep and Read, names affected files, designs an approach, and implements only after approval.
Custom subagents live under `.claude/agents/` and are what `context: fork` and `--agent` run.
In CI, plan mode is also the safe posture: explore and report without any edit capability.
steps.caption: Plan mode is one row in this table, not a separate feature — the exam tests the flag as much as the behaviour.
steps.takeaway: `--permission-mode plan` or `Shift+Tab`. Read-only explore, present, then implement after approval.

steps.title: Gate: add Slack, method undecided
steps.lead: Read what the stem does not say. Three integration methods, materially different consequences, and a task statement that names none of them.
steps.caption: Three integration approaches with different consequences and a task statement that names none: that is the plan-mode trigger.

ask.q: You need to add Slack as a notification channel. The codebase has established patterns for email, SMS and push. Slack offers fundamentally different integration approaches, such as incoming webhooks (one-way), bot tokens (delivery confirmation, programmatic control), or a Slack App (two-way events, workspace approval), and the task says only to add Slack support. Which approach is most effective?
options: Start direct execution using incoming webhooks, matching the existing one-way channel pattern.
Start direct execution by scaffolding a Slack channel class from the existing pattern and defer the integration-method decision.
Start plan mode: explore the integration options and their architectural implications, then present a recommendation before implementing.
Start direct execution with bot tokens, which keeps delivery confirmation available later.
ask.why: Several valid approaches with materially different architectural consequences, plus a requirement that decides nothing, is exactly the plan-mode trigger. Committing to webhooks or to bot tokens decides the trade-off before anyone reviews it, and scaffolding a class before the integration method is chosen builds structure that gets thrown away.

steps.takeaway: Undecided approach plus real consequences means plan mode, however eager the pattern match feels.

steps.title: Where the search output ends up
steps.lead: Now the move that saves the conversation itself. An unfamiliar service, a first reconnaissance pass, and the main thread is already full of directory listings and search results. The fix is not a bigger window.
points: The Explore subagent runs Glob, Grep and Read in its own context and returns a concise summary.
Raw search output stays in that other context, so the main conversation keeps its budget for the actual work.
Built-in subagents: Explore and Plan are read-only and skip CLAUDE.md and git status; general-purpose and claude are the others.
`context: fork` isolates a noisy skill. The Explore subagent isolates a noisy investigation. Same goal, different mechanism.
A larger context window raises the ceiling instead of reducing what is pulled in, and `/compact` has to be repeated.
steps.caption: Watch where the search output lands: inside the subagent's own window, with only a summary crossing back.
steps.takeaway: Noisy reconnaissance goes to Explore. The main window keeps the summary, not the search output.

steps.title: Four signals that force a plan
steps.inshort: More than one file non-trivially, multiple valid approaches, expensive to reverse, or alters architectural shape: any one of these means plan first.
steps.lead: "It is just repetitive edits" is the sentence that gets people. Repetition is not the test; whether decisions remain is. Four signals settle it, and a greenfield build adds a fifth reason to plan.
points: The change touches more than one file non-trivially.
There are multiple valid approaches, so a human must choose before code is written.
It is expensive to reverse, such as a half-finished refactor with broken imports and failing tests.
It alters the architectural shape of the system, which needs a decision, not an edit.
Starting an application from scratch also earns a plan: the blueprint is where better foundations get proposed before any code exists.
Plan mode is the investigation phase, and execution follows after approval. They are sequential, not rivals.
steps.why: The exam classifies a described task as plan or execute, and the traps are scale framing ('it is mechanical') and ceremony framing ('planning always helps'). Naming the four signals lets you answer the classification and reject both traps.
steps.contrast: Treating a large, undecided change as direct execution because the edits repeat is the classic wrong move: the first file locks in an approach the rest then follow, and reverting is costly.
steps.exam: Any of the four signals, or a from-scratch build with real design choices, is a plan-mode stem.
steps.takeaway: If decisions remain, plan. A plan is the bridge to execution, not a rival of it.

steps.title: Gate: repetitive but undecided
steps.inshort: Repetition is not the test; the four signals are.
steps.lead: The word 'repetitive' is the bait. Read past it to how many files, how many approaches, and how expensive a mistake would be.

ask.q: You are asked to extract database queries scattered across a 200-file monolith and move them behind an ORM. The edits look repetitive, the queries have different shapes, and the change touches data-access code across the whole service. Which approach is most effective?
options: Use plan mode to map the affected files and design a phased strategy, then execute the migration.
Start direct execution because the edit is repetitive and Claude can adjust as it goes.
Run an autonomous migration script across all files with no user input.
Build an extensive test suite for every service before choosing any migration approach.
ask.why: More than one file non-trivially, several valid approaches, expensive to reverse and an architectural impact: all four plan-mode signals are present. Repetition does not make the work known. An un-reviewed autonomous rewrite is the failure the plan prevents, and building tests first still leaves the open decision about the migration strategy that planning settles on top of the existing tests.

steps.why: The stem supplies all four plan signals and dresses them as repetitive work.
steps.contrast: 'The edits repeat' invites direct execution, but different query shapes mean the approach is still being decided file by file.
steps.exam: A large multi-file migration with architectural impact is plan mode, however mechanical the edits look.
steps.takeaway: Repetitive edits are not known work. Decisions remaining means plan.

steps.title: Rewording is not a modality change
steps.lead: He rewrote the instruction three times and each attempt is wrong in a different way. That pattern is the tell: prose has failed, and rewriting prose produces different misinterpretations rather than fewer. Change the modality instead.
points: Give two or three concrete input to output pairs. The model generalises from examples far more reliably than from descriptions.
Make the requirement checkable: write the test first, run it to failure, share the failing assertions, fix, repeat until green.
Unfamiliar domain with unknown edge cases: the interview pattern, where Claude asks clarifying questions before implementing.
Test-first wins when requirements are settled but the implementation is wrong. The interview wins when requirements are the gap.
More adjectives, an added reminder and a raised temperature are all the same category of non-fix.
steps.caption: Rewriting prose produces different misinterpretations rather than fewer; only the right panel changes the kind of input.
steps.takeaway: Prose failed repeatedly means show examples, show a failing test, or let Claude ask first.

steps.title: Let Claude ask the questions first
steps.lead: Third modality, and the exam tests the choice sharply. A regulated export on a team that has never built one. Nothing is wrong with the implementation yet, because nobody knows what to specify.
points: Interview pattern: have Claude ask clarifying questions first, so considerations the team does not know it is missing get surfaced.
A prose specification written first encodes the team's blind spots straight into the specification.
Implementing immediately discovers the gaps only after the wrong thing exists.
Input and output examples constrain the shape of the output, which is a different problem from an unknown requirement.
Choose by the gap you have: unknown requirements means interview, known requirements means examples or a failing test.
steps.caption: Follow the cycle: each pass turns an unknown requirement into a known one, which is why a prose spec written first fails.
steps.takeaway: Unknown requirements means let Claude ask first. Known requirements means examples or a test.

steps.title: Drill: coupled defects and stray typos
steps.lead: The stem tells you the two middleware defects interact. That word decides the shape of your feedback. Answer.
steps.caption: Read it left to right: the word interacting puts both defects in a single message and the typos in their own turns.

ask.q: Your auth middleware has two defects that interact: it does not check token expiry, and it returns HTTP 500 instead of 401 for invalid tokens. Fixing the status code changes which branch handles expired tokens, so the two fixes must be decided together. Separately, you have three unrelated typos in the docs. Which approach is most effective?
options: Report all five issues in one message so Claude sees the complete picture.
Report the two middleware defects together in one message, then feed the doc typos back sequentially.
Report the two middleware defects sequentially, one per turn, so each change stays reviewable.
Fix the doc typos first because they are quick, then describe the middleware defects in prose over several turns.
ask.why: Interacting fixes belong in a single message so they are decided consistently, while independent issues are sequenced so each change stays clean and reviewable. One message containing all five mixes coupled and independent work into an undifferentiated request, feeding the coupled defects one at a time lets the first fix invalidate the second, and delaying the coupled change behind unrelated edits adds risk without removing the interaction.

steps.takeaway: Coupled fixes together, independent fixes in sequence. The word interacting decides it.

steps.title: Tighten the standard where it loads
steps.lead: One more failure shape for this task. Integration-test standards keep being ignored, and someone proposes a rules file that bans mocks. Wrong layer: the standard is not enforced because it was never stated where it loads.
points: When a standard is ignored, tighten it where it is loaded: the project `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
Banning mocks in a rules file bans a mechanism instead of stating the standard.
Repeating the goal in the prompt is prose that has already failed.
CLAUDE.md and rules load as context, with no compliance guarantee, so anything that must always apply needs hooks or `permissions.deny`.
That distinction is the whole enforcement story for this domain: memory advises, configuration enforces.
steps.caption: Only the top-right corner enforces anything; banning a mechanism in a rule file leaves the standard itself unstated.
steps.takeaway: State the standard in `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Banning a mechanism in a rule file fixes the symptom.

steps.title: The CI job that waits forever
steps.lead: A pipeline script runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`, the job hangs, and the logs show Claude Code waiting for interactive input. This is the single most tested CI detail in the domain, so learn the flag rather than the workaround.
points: `-p` or `--print` is non-interactive mode: process the prompt, print to stdout, exit. Without it the job waits for a human who never comes.
It is not a timeout problem and not a stdin problem. Raising the timeout still waits forever.
Redirecting `/dev/null` is not the documented headless mode, and it skips print-mode output and exit behaviour.
`CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` does not exist, and there is no `--batch` flag.
Guardrails for a run with no human present: `--max-turns`, `--max-budget-usd`, `--permission-prompts none`, `--no-session-persistence`.
steps.caption: The left column ends the run by itself; the right column either waits longer or reaches for undocumented surface.
steps.code:
claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"
claude -p --max-turns 20 --max-budget-usd 2 --permission-prompts none
steps.takeaway: A job that hangs after the banner is missing `-p`. Not a timeout, not `/dev/null`.

steps.title: Narrative findings do not post themselves
steps.lead: The reviews are substantive but useless downstream, because they arrive as paragraphs a developer pastes into the PR by hand. The team wants each finding posted automatically with file path, line number, severity and suggested fix. Guidance cannot guarantee that shape; a CLI-enforced format can.
points: `--output-format json` gives a machine-parseable payload, and `--json-schema` constrains its shape so every finding has the same fields.
A CLAUDE.md section describing the output format is guidance, so it cannot guarantee structure.
Asking the model in the prompt to return JSON relies on compliance rather than enforcement.
A regex extractor over narrative is brittle and breaks the moment the phrasing shifts.
`--output-format stream-json` is the streaming variant when the CI consumer wants records as they arrive.
steps.caption: Both panels want the same shape of finding; only the right one makes that shape a condition of the output.
steps.takeaway: Automatic inline comments need `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`, not a better description of the format.

steps.title: Gate: the job that never finishes
steps.lead: One flag. The other options treat the symptom or invent surface that does not exist.
steps.caption: Trace the two exits: only the -p branch ends in an exit, and every other option changes the quality of the waiting.

ask.q: Your pipeline script runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`. The job hangs indefinitely, and the logs show Claude Code awaiting interactive input. Which approach is most effective?
options: Increase the job timeout so the process has more time to complete.
Redirect stdin from `/dev/null` so nothing can block the process.
Set `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` in the job environment before invoking the CLI.
Add the `-p` flag so Claude Code runs non-interactively and exits when the prompt completes.
ask.why: `-p`, or `--print`, is the documented non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, prints to stdout and exits without waiting for input. A longer timeout waits just as long because nothing will ever arrive, `/dev/null` is not the documented headless mode and skips print-mode structured output and exit behaviour, and `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is an environment variable that does not exist.

steps.takeaway: `-p` is the fix. Every other option changes the quality of the waiting.

steps.title: The reviewer is not the author
steps.lead: Two people problems in one task, and both have the same shape: a defect that only appears when someone else looks. One is the generator reviewing its own work. The other is a bot commenting on every push until nobody reads it.
points: The generating session keeps its reasoning context and is less likely to question its own decisions, so review must be independent.
Self-review instructions inside the generating session are the failure mode, not the fix.
Duplicate comments on every push are fixed by passing prior findings and reporting only new or still-unaddressed issues.
Full-file review still covers unchanged code: a diff-only pass misses pre-existing issues, and prior findings handle deduplication.
Low-value tests need testing standards and fixtures in `.claude/CLAUDE.md`; duplicate tests need the existing test files in context.
steps.caption: Follow the handoff left to right: the reviewer never sees the reasoning that produced the code.
steps.takeaway: New instance for review, prior findings for deduplication, CLAUDE.md for test standards.

steps.title: Gate: caught only by a colleague
steps.lead: Answer the stem you just read. Every wrong option keeps the same perspective in place and changes something else about it.
steps.caption: The gate is a different perspective, not more effort: re-checking in the same session passes through the same reasoning.

ask.q: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, and non-obvious defects such as performance optimisations that break edge cases, or cleanups that silently change behaviour, are caught only when another person reviews the PR. Claude's own reasoning trace during generation shows it considered those cases and concluded its approach was correct. Which approach is most effective?
options: Run a second, independent Claude Code instance to review the changes without access to the generator's reasoning.
Add a self-review step at the end of generation asking Claude to re-check its own changes.
Reuse the generating session for review, since it already holds all the code context.
Require two developers to review every PR, one of them the author's pair.
ask.why: The generator retains the reasoning context that produced the code and is therefore biased toward its own conclusions, so review must come from an instance without that context, which is why human peer review works. A self-review step is the same session attempting self-critique, reusing the generating session is the anti-pattern the symptom describes, and requiring a second human reviewer leaves the model's blind spot intact.

steps.takeaway: The perspective that produced the code cannot judge it. Independence is the fix.

steps.title: One gate people classify as a memory question
steps.lead: Logging before context is compacted is a hook, not a `CLAUDE.md` instruction. Memory files load as context; hooks are where behaviour is actually enforced. That difference decides this stem.
points: PreCompact fires before context is compacted, which is where a pre-compaction log belongs.
PreToolUse on a Compact event is the tempting wrong answer: there is no such gate.
Rule files and CLAUDE.md carry no compliance guarantee because they are loaded as context.
Behaviour that must always apply belongs to hooks or `permissions.deny`.
Other hooks CI work uses: PostToolUse and PreToolUse for gating a specific tool call.
steps.caption: The log is taken on the way into compaction, at the gate, not reconstructed afterwards.
steps.takeaway: Log before compaction with the PreCompact hook. Memory advises; a hook enforces.

steps.title: The gate the schema unlocks
steps.inshort: Schema'd findings are not the end of the pipeline; a later job reads the severity field and blocks the merge without a human.
steps.lead: Machine-readable output is not the goal in itself; it is the input to the next step. When findings arrive as schema-constrained JSON, a downstream job can parse severity and stop a bad merge on its own.
points: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` makes every finding carry the same fields, so a later step can parse it with `jq` instead of reading prose.
The gate step: if any finding's severity is critical, exit non-zero and block the merge; otherwise let the pipeline continue.
Each step runs in a fresh session, seeded with prior findings, so a review never re-reviews what was already reported.
The project's standards travel into every fresh session through `CLAUDE.md`, so each step starts with review criteria, security policy and testing requirements.

The full sequence: `CLAUDE.md` for context, load prior findings, a fresh session, `-p` for non-interactive execution, `--output-format json --json-schema` for the shape, then act on the findings and block on critical.
steps.code:
claude -p "Review this PR" --output-format json --json-schema review-schema.json > findings.json
jq -e 'any(.findings[]; .severity == "critical")' findings.json && exit 1 || exit 0
steps.why: Prose findings can only be read by a human; schema'd findings can be read by the next job. The exam tests the whole chain, not just the flag that produces the JSON.
steps.contrast: Asking CLAUDE.md to describe the output format keeps the findings readable to a person but not reliably parseable by the next job.
steps.exam: "Block the merge automatically", "read the severity", or "the next step needs structured output" points to `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`.
steps.takeaway: Schema'd findings let a downstream job read severity and block the merge without a human.

steps.title: Gate: the next step cannot read prose
steps.inshort: A machine gate needs schema'd output, not better paragraphs.
steps.lead: The later job has to make a decision on its own. Ask what it can actually read.

ask.q: Your pipeline runs a Claude review step, and a later job must automatically block the merge when any critical finding exists. The review currently returns paragraphs of prose. Which approach is most effective?
options: Run the review with `-p --output-format json --json-schema`, then have the later job parse the severity field and exit non-zero on any critical finding.
Keep the prose review and have the later job scan the text for the word 'critical'.
Describe the exact output format in `CLAUDE.md` so the review returns consistent paragraphs.
Increase the review step's timeout so the model has time to format the findings.
ask.why: `--json-schema` makes the shape a condition of the output, so the downstream job can read severity reliably and block the merge. Scanning prose for a keyword breaks the moment the phrasing shifts; a CLAUDE.md description is guidance rather than enforcement; and the problem is the shape of the output, not the time it has.

steps.why: The downstream job must decide on its own, which requires a shape it can parse.
steps.contrast: Keyword-scanning the prose is the quick fix that works until the model phrases a critical finding differently.
steps.exam: "Automatically block", "parse the severity", "no human reads it" means schema'd output.
steps.takeaway: A gate needs schema'd findings. Prose is for humans, not for the next job.

steps.title: Domain 3 in one breath
steps.lead: That is Domain 3: twenty percent of the exam and the densest configuration surface in it. Three reflexes answer almost every question. Is this file somewhere the team actually receives? Does the standard need to be ambient, or invoked? And does the mechanism enforce, or merely advise?
points: Standards everyone must get live in the committed `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. `~/.claude/` is personal and never reaches a teammate.
Ambient means CLAUDE.md, invoked means a skill, noisy means `context: fork`, unsafe means `allowed-tools`.
A convention for a file pattern is one `.claude/rules/` file with a `paths:` glob, never a copy per directory or a command.
Decisions remaining means plan mode; noisy reconnaissance goes to Explore; prose that fails means examples or a failing test.
A hanging CI job needs `-p`; inline comments need `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`; never self-review.
steps.caption: Three questions in order — who receives it, ambient or invoked, enforce or advise — settle most Domain 3 stems.
steps.takeaway: Who receives it, ambient or invoked, enforce or advise. Three reflexes, most of Domain 3.
